common_name: Costa Rica Blue Salvia (Cool-Toned Deep Blue Anise Sage)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions in spring once soil has warmed, in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: Costa Rica Blue is a taller, more vigorous selection of anise sage than the ubiquitous 'Black and Blue', producing the same jet-black calyces but with flowers in a cooler, more saturated true-blue tone that many Gulf Coast gardeners prize for contrast against warm-colored summer bloomers. Plants build into a substantial 4-6 foot mound by late summer and spread gradually by rhizomes, so give it room or plan to divide it every few years. It flowers continuously from early summer through frost and is one of the most reliable hummingbird plants for the region. Cut the dieback to a few inches after hard frost and mulch the crown, as it returns readily from the roots even after top growth is lost.

common_name: Tequila Sage (Fire-Red Mexican Sage with Black Calyces)

planting.note: Plant in rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil with light shade during peak summer heat; give winter protection or a heavy mulch north of zone 9.

directions: Tequila is a selection of the Mexican cloud-forest species Salvia gesneriiflora prized for intensely saturated, fire-engine red tubular flowers set off by near-black calyces on a large, coarse-textured subshrub. Unlike many tropical salvias it flowers heaviest in fall and into early winter, making it valuable for extending late-season color and hummingbird nectar right up to frost. It performs best with some relief from the hottest afternoon sun in the Gulf South and appreciates consistent soil moisture through summer. Where winters dip below the low 20s F, cut plants back hard after frost and mulch the crown, since they resprout reliably from the base in spring in zones 8b-10.

planting.note: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; stake or site against a wall where wind might topple the tall flowering stems.

directions: Limelight is a striking selection of Mexican sage grown as much for its acid-green calyces as for the deep violet-purple flowers that emerge from them, creating a two-tone effect unusual among salvias. It grows into a large, architectural back-of-border subshrub that stays vegetative through summer heat and puts on its main flower show in fall as days shorten, often continuing until the first hard freeze. Because it can reach 6-8 feet with an open, somewhat leggy habit, it benefits from a spring pinch or two to encourage branching and from a position sheltered from strong wind. In zone 8 it usually dies back to the ground in winter and returns vigorously from the roots once soil warms in spring.

common_name: Betsy Clebsch Vermillion Sage (Floriferous Orange-Red Hummingbird Salvia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings and set out in spring in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Named for California salvia expert Betsy Clebsch, this selection of vermillion sage is noted for producing an even heavier flush of clear scarlet-orange flowers than the straight species, on a slightly more compact frame that fits neatly into a mixed perennial border. Like the species it is native to dry limestone slopes in the Sierra Madre Oriental and shares its excellent drought and heat tolerance once roots are established, making it a low-water, high-reward choice for Gulf Coast xeriscaping. Hummingbirds visit it constantly through its long bloom season, which runs from late spring to frost in mild climates. Cut plants back by a third in early spring to keep growth dense and to remove winter-damaged stems.

common_name: Wild Watermelon Salvia (Vivid Watermelon-Pink Baby Sage)

planting.note: Plant in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants tolerate reflected heat and short dry spells well.

directions: Wild Watermelon is a compact baby sage selection valued for saturated, deep pink-magenta flowers produced in nearly continuous flushes from late spring through fall, set against small aromatic leaves that give off a fruity scent when brushed. It forms a tidy rounded mound smaller than most autumn sage cultivars, making it useful for the front of a border or in containers, and it draws hummingbirds and bees reliably throughout its long bloom season. It tolerates heat, humidity, and short dry spells once established, needing supplemental water mainly during extended drought. Shear lightly after each major bloom flush and cut back by a third in early spring to keep growth compact and encourage the heaviest flowering.
